title: Leadership Is a Social System
question: If leadership is partly something followers and observers construct, what can a leader actually do to earn trust, develop people and be understood?

overview.text: Leadership is usually taught as a property of a person: a style, a set of traits, a presence. This week treats it as a property of relationships and of systems. The research on leadership styles is weaker than its popularity suggests, and observers routinely credit or blame leaders for outcomes they only partly control. What remains robust is narrower and more useful: leaders shape whether people trust them, whether bad news travels upward, whether feedback improves work or provokes defense, and whether a recommendation is understood by the people who must act on it.

The four lessons move from evidence to practice. Lesson 1 asks what leadership research can and cannot tell you. Lesson 2 examines trust and psychological safety — the conditions under which people tell you the truth. Lesson 3 turns to feedback, coaching, delegation and accountability: how to manage through others when the classic finding is that feedback often backfires. Lesson 4 addresses executive communication and the slippery idea of executive presence.

The Leadership Conversation Simulator lets you rehearse a hard conversation with a high performer who undermines colleagues. The case, The Brilliant Analyst, puts these ideas under pressure: a technically superior recommendation that fails to win adoption. The assignment asks you to write one recommendation three ways — memo, one-page brief and 60-second verbal version — the most transferable skill in this course.

objectives: Evaluate claims about leadership styles using the meta-analytic evidence and its measurement critique.
Diagnose trust problems with the ability–benevolence–integrity model and distinguish psychological safety from comfort.
Design feedback, delegation and accountability so that they keep attention on the task and make expectations explicit.
Conduct a difficult conversation that holds a clear standard while managing defensiveness.
Write one recommendation as an analytical memo, a one-page brief and a 60-second verbal explanation, each fit for its audience.

lessons.title: What Leadership Research Can and Cannot Tell You
lessons.summary: Leadership research offers real but modest findings, and much of what passes for leadership knowledge is attribution after the fact.
objectives: Compare the main families of leadership theory by their core claim, typical evidence and main weakness.
Explain the romance of leadership and predict when it will distort evaluations of a leader.
Interpret meta-analytic leadership correlations alongside the measurement critique that challenges them.
lessons.executive: Leadership matters, but less precisely than the industry around it claims. Observers systematically over-credit and over-blame leaders, especially after extreme outcomes. The best-known meta-analysis finds that transformational leadership correlates about .44 with outcomes — yet a plain transactional behavior, rewarding people for meeting agreed goals, comes close behind. Critics argue that popular leadership questionnaires partly measure the outcomes they claim to predict. For an executive this means: judge leaders on specific, observable behaviors and on process, not on reputations built from results; be skeptical of programs that promise to install a “style”; and expect your own reputation to swing with outcomes you only partly control.

explore.text: Consider two hypothetical hospital chief executives. Both inherit similar regional systems, both make broadly similar decisions, and both are respected by their staffs. In the first system, a competitor closes and patient volumes jump; in the second, a reimbursement change cuts revenue. Within two years the first executive is described in the trade press as a visionary and the second as a leader who lost the room. Nothing in their behavior changed. The outcomes did, and the story about leadership followed the outcomes.

You have seen the same pattern in technology companies, where a founder is a genius during a funding boom and an obstacle during a downturn; in politics, where a governor is credited with an economy that national conditions mostly drove; and in professional sports, where a manager’s tactical reputation tracks the team’s record far more closely than any observer could justify from the decisions themselves. The question for this lesson is uncomfortable: how much of what we call leadership is a cause of results, and how much is a story we tell about results?

Before reading on, write down a leader you admire and a leader you consider weak. For each, list what you actually observed them do, and separately what outcomes you associate with them. Which list did your judgment rest on?

understand.text: Leadership research has moved through several families of theory. None has been simply refuted, and none has delivered the precise, portable recipe the management-book market implies. It helps to see them side by side, with the kind of evidence each relies on and the weakness that each carries.

understand.caption: Families of leadership theory: what each claims and where each is weak
rows: Some stable characteristics make people more likely to emerge as, or be effective as, leaders.
Correlations between personality or ability measures and leader emergence or ratings.
Modest correlations; emergence (being seen as a leader) is not the same as effectiveness.
What leaders do matters more than who they are: consideration for people and structuring of work.
Follower questionnaires about leader behavior, related to satisfaction and performance.
Usually the same people rate the behavior and the outcome.
The best behavior depends on the situation: task structure, follower readiness, authority.
Field and lab studies testing situation × behavior interactions.
Interactions are hard to replicate; many popular contingency models have thin empirical support.
Leaders who articulate a vision, model values and stimulate followers produce performance beyond expectations.
Large literature using standard questionnaires; meta-analyses show sizable correlations.
Construct defined partly by its effects; measurement structure disputed.
Leaders form relationships of different quality with different followers, and relationship quality matters.
Dyadic surveys of relationship quality and outcomes.
Mostly correlational; high-quality exchange may follow good performance rather than cause it.
Leadership is partly an inference observers make to explain outcomes.
Archival and experimental studies of how people assign credit and blame.
Shows inflated attributions, not that leaders have no effect.
understand.note: APERTURE synthesis. Evidence descriptions are general characterizations of each literature; see the cited sources for specific findings.

understand.text: The attribution family deserves particular attention because it explains why the others are hard to study. Meindl and colleagues described a *romance of leadership*: people prefer to explain organizational outcomes by pointing to leaders, and this preference strengthens when outcomes are extreme. A very good or very bad year produces more leadership talk, not because leadership changed but because observers need an explanation and leaders are the most visible candidate.

The strongest positive evidence for a leadership style comes from meta-analysis. Judge and Piccolo pooled 626 correlations from 87 sources on the “full-range” model. Transformational leadership showed an overall validity of .44 with criteria such as follower satisfaction, motivation and rated leader effectiveness. Contingent reward — the transactional practice of agreeing on goals and rewarding their achievement — came next at .39 and was the stronger predictor for several criteria. Laissez-faire leadership, the absence of leadership, was negatively related at −.37.

understand.caption: Overall meta-analytic validities of three leadership dimensions (correlation with combined criteria)
understand.note: Values from the abstract of Judge & Piccolo (2004). Correlations, not causal effects.

blocks.text: A correlation (r) runs from −1 to +1 and describes how closely two measures move together. Squaring it gives the share of variance in one measure that is statistically associated with the other: .44 squared is about .19, or roughly a fifth. That is large by the standards of social science, but it leaves four fifths of the variation in the outcome associated with other things. It also says nothing yet about direction: a correlation between leader ratings and team outcomes is equally consistent with leaders improving teams and with successful teams rating their leaders more generously.

A meta-analytic correlation is an average across many studies, often corrected for measurement error. Its precision depends on the quality of the studies it pools. Week 4’s tools — confounding, reverse causation, common-method bias — apply here directly.

understand.text: Two practical points follow even before any critique. First, the gap between transformational and contingent-reward leadership is small. The unglamorous discipline of setting clear expectations and following through is not a lesser form of leadership. Second, the strongest single finding is about absence: leaders who avoid decisions and withdraw from problems are associated with worse outcomes. Much of the practical value of leadership research is a warning against abdication rather than a formula for inspiration.

challenge.text: The transformational literature faces a fundamental methodological challenge. Van Knippenberg and Sitkin reviewed the research and identified four problems: the construct lacks a clear definition, the causal model linking it to outcomes is underspecified, the construct is confounded with its effects, and the dominant questionnaires do not reproduce the dimensional structure the theory claims. Their recommendation was to abandon the umbrella construct and study more precisely defined behaviors. Defenders point to the consistency of meta-analytic associations such as those in Judge and Piccolo. The live disagreement is not whether the correlations exist but what they mean.

The confounding problem is easiest to see with an example. Suppose a questionnaire asks whether your leader “inspires you to perform beyond expectations.” If you answer yes, you have partly reported an outcome — your extra effort — not only a behavior. Correlating that answer with your effort is then partly correlating a measure with itself. A behavior-based item would ask instead whether the leader explained the reasons for a decision or asked for your view before deciding, which an outside observer could verify.

Combine this with the romance of leadership and a troubling loop appears. If followers who experience success attribute it to their leader, they may rate that leader as more inspiring, and the rating will then “predict” the success that produced it. This is APERTURE’s synthesis of the two critiques, not a finding from either paper, but it explains why rating-based leadership research can look stronger than the underlying causal effect.

challenge.title: Methodological note: three reasons leadership effects are hard to estimate

items: **Common-source variance.** When the same person rates the leader and the outcome, a general positive or negative impression inflates the correlation.

**Selection.** Leaders are not randomly assigned to teams. Strong leaders may be given strong teams, or troubled units may be handed to turnaround specialists, biasing comparisons in either direction.

**Outcome noise.** In settings with large random variation, such as quarterly earnings, a single season or a small hospital’s mortality rate, the signal from a leader’s decisions is swamped, and observers fill the gap with attribution.

blocks.text: The strongest designs avoid these problems with behavior coded by outsiders, objective outcomes measured independently, and some exogenous variation in who leads — for example, a rotation rule or an unexpected departure. Such designs are rare, which is why a careful reader holds leadership-style findings more loosely than findings in, say, personnel selection.

challenge.text: None of this implies that leaders do not matter. It implies that we know less about *which* behaviors matter, *how much*, and *where* than the confidence of leadership training suggests. The working stance for an executive is to treat named styles as loose bundles of behaviors and to focus on the specific behaviors whose effects are plausible and observable: setting clear goals, following through on commitments, giving task-focused feedback, making decisions rather than avoiding them, and building relationships of consistent quality across a team.

apply.text: A hypothetical software company replaces its engineering vice president after two missed launch dates. The new leader arrives as a cloud vendor resolves an outage that had caused both slips, and the next launch ships on time. Within a quarter, internal surveys show sharply higher ratings of the new leader’s vision and communication. A board member proposes building the company’s leadership curriculum around her style. The romance-of-leadership analysis asks first what changed in the environment, then what she specifically did differently, and only then whether those behaviors are teachable.

In a hypothetical military logistics command, two unit commanders are compared on readiness scores. One unit sits next to the main depot; the other is supplied across a mountain route. A fair evaluation separates what the commander controls — maintenance discipline, the quality of after-action reviews, how quickly problems are surfaced — from what the route controls. The same logic applies to a law-firm practice leader whose group benefits from a regulatory wave, or a consulting partner whose client base happens to be in a growing industry.

In player development the pattern is constant. A coordinator whose affiliates produce several breakout prospects in one season is often credited with a method; one whose prospects stagnate is suspected of weak coaching. With small numbers of players, large random variation in development, and talent that was largely determined at acquisition, these outcomes are poor evidence about the coaching. A better evaluation looks at process: the quality of individual development plans, whether coaching cues were consistent across staff, how quickly problems were escalated, and what players and peers can describe the coordinator actually doing.

apply.title: Executive twist: a vendor offers a leadership program with a 30% performance claim

blocks.text: A training vendor presents a slide stating that managers who completed its transformational leadership program saw their teams’ engagement and performance scores rise 30% within a year. You have a limited development budget and a skeptical finance partner. You cannot see the underlying data before the decision.

items: Who rated performance and engagement, and were they the same people who rated the managers before and after?
Which managers enrolled — volunteers, high-potentials, or a random subset — and what happened to comparable managers who did not enroll?
Over the same year, what happened to the organization’s performance as a whole?
Which specific behaviors does the program change, and how would an outside observer see them?
What would a small, staged pilot with a comparison group cost relative to the full program?

blocks.text: None of these questions requires hostility to development. They separate a program that changes behaviors from a program that changes ratings.

retain.text: Leadership research supports a modest, behavior-focused view: leaders who set clear expectations, follow through and stay engaged are associated with better outcomes, and abdication is clearly harmful. Grand style labels are weaker than they look, partly because the measures are contaminated by outcomes and partly because observers romanticize leaders after extreme results. Judge leaders, including yourself, on observable behavior and decision process.
From memory: what are the four problems van Knippenberg and Sitkin identified in charismatic–transformational research?
Why does an extreme season or quarter make leadership attributions stronger rather than more accurate?
Name one leader you evaluate regularly. Write two behavior-based questions you could answer about them without looking at results.

takeaways: Observers over-attribute outcomes to leaders, most of all after extreme results.
Transformational leadership correlates about .44 with outcomes, but contingent reward is close behind; abdication is clearly harmful.
Leadership questionnaires can measure outcomes as well as behavior, inflating apparent effects.
Evaluate leaders on specific, observable behaviors and decision process, not on reputations built from results.

lessons.title: Trust and Psychological Safety: The Conditions for Hearing the Truth
lessons.summary: Trust is a willingness to be vulnerable built on perceived ability, benevolence and integrity; psychological safety is a team’s shared belief that speaking up will not be punished — and neither is the same as comfort.
objectives: Diagnose a trust problem using the ability–benevolence–integrity model.
Distinguish psychological safety from niceness, low standards and interpersonal trust.
Evaluate the strength and limits of the evidence linking psychological safety to learning and performance.
lessons.executive: Leaders rarely fail for lack of information that exists somewhere in the organization; they fail because the information never reaches them. Two ideas explain why. Trust is a willingness to accept vulnerability to someone, and it rests on three separate perceptions: that the person is able, that they care about your interests, and that they act on principles you accept. Psychological safety is a team’s shared belief that admitting errors or raising concerns will not be punished. Both are associated with learning and better performance in correlational research, though causation is not established. Neither means comfort: the goal is high candor combined with high standards.

explore.text: A hypothetical night shift on a hospital ward. A newly hired nurse notices that a medication dose on a chart looks high for the patient’s weight. The attending physician who wrote it is known to be brilliant and impatient. Calling him at 2 a.m. risks being wrong, being dismissed, and being remembered as the nurse who questioned him. Not calling risks harm to a patient. Most of what determines her choice was settled long before that night: by how the physician reacted the last time someone questioned him, and by what the ward has learned about the cost of speaking up.

Every organization runs this experiment constantly. A junior associate notices a problem in a merger agreement drafted by a partner. An engineer sees that a deployment schedule will skip a test. An analyst suspects that a model favored by the head of the department is overfit. A coach sees a player compensating for discomfort the player has not reported. In each case the question is whether information moves upward, and the answer depends less on the individual’s courage than on what the system has taught them.
Think of the last time you learned about a serious problem later than you should have. Who knew earlier, and what would they have had to risk to tell you?

understand.text: Trust as willingness to be vulnerable

Mayer, Davis and Schoorman defined trust as a willingness to be vulnerable to another party based on the expectation that the other will perform an action important to you, regardless of your ability to monitor or control them. The definition separates trust itself from the reasons for it. Those reasons — the perceived *trustworthiness* of the other party — have three factors: **ability** (competence in the relevant domain), **benevolence** (the belief that the other cares about your interests beyond their own gain), and **integrity** (the belief that the other adheres to principles you find acceptable and applies them consistently).

understand.caption: Trust formation in the integrative model

steps.label: Trustor’s propensity
steps.text: A general disposition to trust others, most influential when you know little about the other party.

steps.label: Perceived trustworthiness
steps.text: Ability, benevolence and integrity, judged separately.

steps.label: Trust
steps.text: Willingness to accept vulnerability to this party.

steps.label: Risk-taking in the relationship
steps.text: You delegate, disclose, defer or depend on them.

steps.label: Outcomes
steps.text: What happens updates your perceptions of ability, benevolence and integrity.

understand.text: The model is useful because it turns a vague complaint — “I don’t trust him” — into a diagnosis. You can trust a colleague’s integrity and doubt their ability in a new domain. You can respect a leader’s ability and suspect that they do not care what happens to you. Each deficit calls for a different response: ability is addressed by demonstrated competence or a change of role; benevolence by visible behavior that costs the leader something on the other person’s behalf; integrity by consistency between words and actions over time. The feedback loop matters too. Trust grows only when someone takes a risk and the outcome confirms it, so trust cannot be built without exposure.

understand.title: Prerequisite: trust is relational and specific

blocks.text: In everyday speech trust is a global feeling. In the model it is specific: trust in *this* person, for *this* kind of action. You may trust a surgeon with your appendix and not with your investments. When diagnosing a breakdown, always ask “trusted to do what?” A new executive who is trusted to make technical calls may not yet be trusted to make personnel decisions, and treating those as one thing produces surprises.

understand.text: Psychological safety as a team climate

Edmondson introduced *team psychological safety* as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — asking questions, admitting mistakes, raising concerns, proposing unpopular ideas. In a study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company, psychological safety was associated with team learning behavior, and learning behavior mediated the relationship between psychological safety and team performance. Team efficacy — confidence in the team’s ability — was not associated with learning once psychological safety was taken into account. The study also pointed to structures that shape safety, including context support and team-leader coaching.

Psychological safety differs from trust in two ways. It is a property of a group rather than of a pair, and it concerns the consequences of speaking up rather than confidence that another person will act in your interest. A team can contain pairs who trust each other and still have a climate in which nobody challenges the leader in meetings.

understand.caption: Psychological safety is not low standards: a 2×2 of safety and performance demands
cells: Disengagement: little is expected and little is said; problems persist quietly.
Comfort: people speak freely, but little is at stake and learning is shallow.
Anxiety: high expectations with high fear; errors are hidden and bad news travels slowly.
Learning: high expectations with candor; errors surface early and are worked on.
understand.note: APERTURE teaching device. A popular framing in practitioner writing; the four labels are descriptive, not empirically derived categories.

understand.text: The evidence base has grown well beyond the original study. Frazier and colleagues meta-analyzed 136 independent samples covering more than 22,000 individuals and nearly 5,000 groups. They compared the relative strength of antecedents, tested whether psychological safety predicts task performance and citizenship behavior beyond positive leader relations and work engagement, and examined whether study design and national culture changed the results. The synthesis supports psychological safety as a robust correlate of learning and performance-related outcomes across many settings.

challenge.text: Three cautions keep this material honest. First, most of the evidence is correlational. Teams that perform well may feel safer because success reduces the cost of admitting errors; the arrow can run backward. Meta-analysis aggregates the evidence but does not convert correlations into causal estimates. Second, the popular version of psychological safety has drifted toward “being nice” and avoiding discomfort, which is close to the opposite of the construct: safety exists so that uncomfortable information can be said. Third, a climate can be safe for the majority and unsafe for those with the least status, which a team-average score can hide.

There is a live question about how much psychological safety adds beyond related constructs such as good leader relationships and engagement. Frazier and colleagues tested exactly this incremental question, and the original study found that safety, not team efficacy, tracked learning behavior. Yet the field’s measures are overwhelmingly self-reports from the same people who report the outcomes, and the causal link from a leader’s behavior to safety to performance has been demonstrated far less often than it is asserted in practitioner writing.

blocks.text: Psychological safety is measured by asking individuals and then aggregating their answers to the team. That move is justified only if members agree with each other reasonably well; otherwise the average describes nobody. Researchers check agreement statistically before aggregating. For a leader the lesson is practical: the average score on an engagement or safety survey is less informative than the spread. A team where most people feel safe and two people do not is not a safe team for those two, and they are often the ones holding the information you need.
Trust research has a parallel issue. Trust is directional — you may trust me more than I trust you — so asking only one side of a relationship can mislead.

challenge.text: Trust has its own failure mode. Because trust means accepting vulnerability without monitoring, high trust can reduce oversight exactly where oversight is needed. Financial fraud cases and research misconduct cases often involve a trusted, highly able person whose work was not checked because checking felt like an accusation. The mature position is that good systems verify everyone’s work routinely, so verification signals process rather than suspicion.

apply.text: Software teams that run blameless post-incident reviews offer a concrete design. After an outage, the review reconstructs what each person knew and why their actions made sense at the time, and it asks what in the system allowed the error, rather than who should be punished. The standard stays high — the outage is treated as serious — while the cost of honest reporting falls. Military after-action reviews use a similar structure: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to sustain or change.

In a hypothetical law firm, a practice leader wants associates to flag drafting errors in partners’ work. Announcing an open-door policy changes little. What changes behavior is a partner publicly thanking an associate for catching an error in the partner’s own draft, and the associate seeing no cost at the next assignment decision. The ability–benevolence–integrity lens explains why: associates already believe partners are able; what they doubt is benevolence when status is threatened.

In player development the information that most needs to travel upward is often the most personally risky to share: a pitcher’s discomfort that might cost a promotion, a hitter’s loss of confidence, a coach’s disagreement with an organizational directive, an analyst’s doubt about a model a senior leader favors. A leader who wants that information has to make it cheaper to disclose than to conceal — by separating injury reporting from evaluation where possible, by responding to bad news with questions before judgments, and by visibly acting on what is raised. Bilingual and cross-cultural staffs add a further layer: what counts as respectful disagreement varies, and a silence can mean agreement in one context and deference in another.
Listening and questioning as trust behaviors

items: **Ask before you assert.** Opening a difficult topic with a genuine question (“What are you seeing that I might be missing?”) signals that disagreement is wanted. It works only if you can tolerate the answer.
**Respond to the first bad news well.** People test safety with a small disclosure. Your reaction to that test sets the price of the next one.
**Close the loop.** Tell people what you did with what they raised, including when you decided not to act and why. Integrity is judged on consistency between what you invite and what you do.
**Make your own errors visible.** Describing a mistake you made and what you changed lowers the status cost of others doing the same.

apply.title: Executive twist: the engagement survey that looks fine

blocks.text: Your department’s annual climate survey shows high average agreement with “It is safe to take a risk on this team.” Two weeks later you learn that a significant data error persisted for months because the person who found it did not want to embarrass the colleague responsible. You have no item-level data from the survey and limited time. What do you conclude? A reasonable reading is that the survey measured the comfort of the majority, not the safety of the person holding inconvenient information. Treat the incident as better evidence about your climate than the survey average, and ask how disagreement is handled in your own meetings before you ask about anyone else’s.

retain.text: Trust is a willingness to be vulnerable, built from separate judgments of ability, benevolence and integrity and updated by outcomes when someone takes a risk. Psychological safety is a team’s shared belief that interpersonal risk is safe; it is a robust correlate of learning and performance, though causal evidence is thinner than its popularity. Neither is comfort: the target is candor under high standards.

Give one reason the correlation between psychological safety and performance might run in the opposite direction from the usual story.
What did you do the last time someone brought you bad news? What did it teach them about the price of the next disclosure?

takeaways: Trust is willingness to be vulnerable; trustworthiness has three separable parts: ability, benevolence and integrity.
Psychological safety is a team-level belief that speaking up is safe — not niceness, not low standards.
Evidence links safety to learning and performance, mostly correlationally; causation is often asserted rather than shown.
Leaders set the price of disclosure through how they respond to the first piece of bad news.

lessons.title: Coaching, Feedback and Managing Through Others
lessons.summary: Feedback helps on average but often backfires when it targets the person rather than the task, and leading through others means designing delegation and accountability, not only delivering messages.
objectives: Explain why a substantial share of feedback interventions reduce performance, using feedback intervention theory.
Structure a difficult conversation that keeps attention on the task and lowers defensiveness.
Match a level of delegation to a person’s demonstrated readiness and the stakes of the decision.
Judge what coaching meta-analyses can and cannot tell you about a coaching program.
lessons.executive: Most managers assume feedback is reliably good and that more is better. The largest classic meta-analysis disagrees: feedback improves performance on average, but a substantial share of feedback interventions made performance worse. The mechanism is attention. Feedback that pulls attention toward the self — praise or criticism of the person, comparisons that threaten status — competes with the task; feedback that points to the task and the next step helps. Workplace coaching shows positive average effects in meta-analysis, from a small and imperfect literature. As a senior leader your leverage is less in delivering feedback yourself than in designing how your managers delegate, follow up and hold people accountable.

explore.text: Predict the answer before reading on. Researchers gathered studies in which people received feedback about their performance and compared them with similar people who did not. Across all those studies, what share of feedback interventions do you think made performance *worse* than no feedback at all? Most managers guess a small number, under one in ten.
Write down your estimate, and one reason feedback might make someone perform worse.

Kluger and DeNisi’s review and meta-analysis found that feedback interventions improved performance on average, but that the results were highly variable and a substantial share of interventions — more than a third in their analysis — reduced performance. The finding was not that feedback is useless. It was that the same act can help or harm depending on where it directs the recipient’s attention.

A hypothetical radiology department introduced a monthly dashboard ranking each physician’s report turnaround time against colleagues. Turnaround improved for some, but several of the most careful readers began to rush, and the conversation in the department shifted from “how do we read this kind of scan better” to “who is at the bottom of the list.” The feedback was accurate. What it drew attention to was status.

understand.text: Feedback intervention theory

Kluger and DeNisi proposed that behavior is regulated by comparing performance with standards, and that attention is limited. Feedback works by moving attention among levels: the details of the task, the motivation to perform the task, and the self — one’s identity, competence and standing. Feedback that keeps attention on the task and on how to close the gap tends to improve performance. Feedback that moves attention to the self tends to weaken or reverse the effect, because cognitive resources go to protecting self-image instead of improving the work.

understand.caption: How a feedback message can help or harm (feedback intervention theory, simplified)

steps.label: Feedback message
steps.text: Information that performance differs from a standard.

steps.label: Where attention goes
steps.text: Toward the task and next step, or toward the self and one’s standing.

steps.label: Task focus
steps.text: Effort and strategy adjust to close the gap; performance tends to improve.

steps.label: Self focus
steps.text: Energy goes to defending identity, discounting the source or disengaging; performance can fall.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what “a share of interventions reduced performance” means

blocks.text: A meta-analysis reports an average effect and the spread of effects around it. A positive average with a wide spread means that some interventions helped a lot and others hurt. An average tells you what to expect from a typical intervention drawn at random; the spread tells you that design choices matter enormously. When a meta-analysis finds both, the practical question is not “does feedback work?” but “what distinguishes the interventions that work from those that backfire?”

understand.caption: Task-focused versus self-focused feedback: the same issue, two ways
rows: “The recommendation appears on slide 14. Move it to slide 1 and cut slides 6–9; the client asked one question.”
“Two pending labs weren’t in the handoff. Use the checklist’s pending section before you leave.”
“Your peers think you’re arrogant in reviews.”
“In Tuesday’s review you rejected three suggestions without asking why they were made. Ask one question before you reject.”
“Your summary let the committee decide in ten minutes because you gave the trade-off first.”

understand.text: Coaching

Coaching is a longer relationship in which feedback is one ingredient among goal setting, questioning and practice. Jones, Woods and Guillaume’s meta-analysis of workplace coaching found positive average effects on learning and performance outcomes, with variation across outcomes and arrangements. The research base is small relative to the size of the coaching industry, and many studies rely on self-reported outcomes.
Delegation and accountability

Managing through others is mostly design, not conversation. A senior leader has more influence through how decisions are delegated and how follow-up works than through any single feedback talk. Delegation is not binary. It runs along a continuum, and the right point depends on the person’s demonstrated readiness in this specific kind of decision and on the cost of an error. The table below is a practitioner heuristic, not a validated instrument; similar continua appear in many management texts.

understand.caption: A delegation continuum (practitioner heuristic)
rows: Novice in this domain, high stakes, no time.
Building judgment; you want to see their reasoning.
“Decide, but check with me before acting.”
Reasoning is sound; stakes still high.
“Decide and act; tell me what you did.”
Track record in this domain; reversible decisions.
“It’s yours; I’ll ask about results quarterly.”
Proven in this domain; you will not second-guess.
understand.note: APERTURE synthesis of common practitioner delegation continua. Not empirically calibrated.

understand.text: Accountability, in this frame, is the agreement about what success looks like, who decides, and when the conversation about results happens — made explicit before the work starts. Many accountability failures are delegation failures in disguise: the person thought they were at level 4 and the manager thought level 2. The most common leadership error at senior levels is not harshness; it is ambiguity followed by disappointment.

challenge.text: Several limits apply. The feedback meta-analysis drew heavily on laboratory and narrow tasks; a manager’s conversation with a senior employee involves relationships, careers and politics that the coded interventions did not. The coaching meta-analysis rests on few studies, often without random assignment, and people who seek or are offered coaching may differ from those who are not. Neither literature tells you which specific coaching method works best.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why coaching studies are hard to run well

items: **Selection.** Organizations offer coaching to high-potentials or to people in trouble; either way the coached group differs from the comparison group before coaching starts.
**Self-report.** The coachee, who invested time and may like the coach, often rates the outcome.
**No placebo.** Any attention from a senior person may help, so it is hard to separate the method from the attention.
**Publication filter.** Studies by providers with positive results are more likely to be written up.

blocks.text: A careful buyer asks for objective outcomes, a comparison group, and the share of participants who did not improve.

challenge.text: *Feedforward* — asking for suggestions about the future rather than evaluations of the past — is a popular practitioner technique. Its logic fits feedback intervention theory: future-oriented suggestions keep attention on the next task and away from defending past performance. APERTURE treats it as a plausible design idea with a thin evidence base, not an established finding.

There is also a values tension. Purely task-focused feedback can become cold, and some people need to hear that their standing is secure before they can attend to the task. The relational context from [the previous lesson](#w05-l2) matters: the same sentence lands differently from a manager whose benevolence is trusted than from one whose benevolence is in doubt.

apply.caption: A five-step structure for a hard feedback conversation (practitioner heuristic)

steps.label: Purpose
steps.text: State why you are meeting and what you want for them.

steps.label: Observation
steps.text: Describe a specific, verifiable behavior — what you saw or heard, when.

steps.label: Impact
steps.text: Explain the effect on the work or on others, without labeling the person.

steps.label: Inquiry
steps.text: Ask for their view and listen; you may be missing context.

steps.label: Agreement
steps.text: Agree on a specific next behavior and a date to review it.

apply.text: Defensiveness is the predictable response when a message threatens identity. You cannot prevent it, but you can lower the threat: keep observations specific and verifiable rather than characterological, acknowledge what is valuable about the person’s work without using it as a sweetener that buries the message, and allow silence after the hard sentence. If the person says “So you think I’m the problem,” a useful reply separates identity from behavior: “I think your analysis is the best on the team. I’m talking about one behavior in reviews that is costing you influence.”

In a hypothetical consulting firm, a manager delegates a client workshop to a senior associate “to run.” The associate redesigns the agenda; the manager, embarrassed in front of the partner, overrides it on the morning of the workshop. Both experience the other as untrustworthy. The repair is not a feedback conversation about the associate’s judgment; it is a conversation about the delegation level that was never stated.

Defensiveness looks different by setting, which is why the structure matters more than a script. In a hypothetical federal agency, a program manager told that her contractor oversight is weak hears a threat to her clearance-review record and responds with documentation of every meeting she held. Arguing about the documentation goes nowhere. What moves the conversation is narrowing it to one observable gap — two invoices approved without the required deliverable check — and asking what made that check hard to do. Often the answer reveals a system problem, such as an approval queue that rewards speed, which the leader can fix and which makes the behavioral request credible.

Player development is coaching at two levels. Coaches coach players, and directors and coordinators coach coaches. Feedback intervention theory applies to both. A player told “you lack mental toughness” receives self-focused feedback; one told “after a two-strike foul your setup widens; let’s rehearse resetting your stance” receives task-focused feedback. A coordinator who corrects a coach in front of players makes the correction about status. Delegation clarity matters just as much: an affiliate coach who believes he owns a player’s plan while the organization believes he is executing it will experience every adjustment from above as distrust.

apply.title: Executive twist: the high performer who undermines peers

blocks.text: Your most productive direct report delivers outstanding work and is frequently dismissive of colleagues in meetings; two people have asked to move off her projects. You have no formal complaint, some colleagues privately admire her, and losing her would hurt a key deliverable. A clean answer does not exist. The task-focused path is to name specific behaviors and their costs, make an explicit agreement, and follow up — accepting a risk that she leaves. The alternative, waiting, is also a decision: it tells everyone else what the organization values. The simulator this week lets you test these trade-offs.

retain.text: Feedback helps on average but backfires often, and the difference lies largely in where it sends attention: toward the task and the next step, or toward the self. Coaching shows positive average effects from an imperfect literature. Managing through others depends on explicit delegation levels and accountability agreements, made before the work starts.
Explain, in two sentences, why accurate feedback can reduce performance.
Rewrite a piece of feedback you gave recently so that it is specific, task-focused and ends with an agreed next step.
For one person who reports to you, which delegation level do you think they are at, and which level do they think they are at?

Feedback that draws attention to the self tends to weaken effects; task-focused feedback with a next step tends to help.
Coaching meta-analysis shows positive average effects, from a small, largely self-report literature.
Many accountability failures are unstated delegation levels; agree on who decides before the work starts.

lessons.title: Executive Communication and the Question of Presence
lessons.summary: Senior audiences need the recommendation first, the reasoning they will test, and the decision they must make; “executive presence” is better understood as other people’s inferences about your judgment and trustworthiness than as a trait.
objectives: Structure a recommendation so the decision and the reason appear before the supporting analysis.
Analyze an audience’s concerns, decision rights and prior beliefs before choosing content and format.
Adapt one recommendation into memo, brief and verbal forms without changing its substance.
Separate what research supports about “executive presence” from practitioner claims.
lessons.executive: Analysts write in the order they discovered things; executives need to read in the order they will decide. Put the recommendation and its main reason first, then the reasoning the audience will challenge, then the evidence — and say what decision you need and by when. These are practitioner disciplines, not laboratory findings, but they rest on a sound principle: busy readers ration attention. “Executive presence” has little rigorous research behind it as a construct. What research does support is that observers infer leadership from outcomes and impressions, and that trust rests on perceived ability, benevolence and integrity. Presence is mostly earned by being clear, consistent and right about what matters.

explore.text: A hypothetical chief operating officer of a regional bank opens a 42-slide deck from her analytics team. Slide 1 is the agenda; slides 2 to 9 describe the data sources; the recommendation — close eleven branches and redeploy staff to a lending center — appears on slide 31. She stops at slide 4 and asks, “What do you want me to do?” The analyst, who has spent six weeks on the work, feels the question as a dismissal. The executive meant it literally.

The mismatch is structural. The analyst’s natural order is the order of discovery: question, data, method, findings, recommendation. The executive’s natural order is the order of decision: what am I being asked to decide, why should I agree, what could go wrong, and what do I do next. Neither order is wrong. Using the discovery order with a decision audience simply makes the audience do the synthesis, and most will not.
Pull up the last recommendation you wrote. In which sentence does the recommendation first appear? What would a reader who stopped after the first paragraph believe you wanted?

understand.text: Answer first: BLUF and the pyramid

Two practitioner frameworks formalize the answer-first order. **BLUF** — bottom line up front — is a convention from U.S. military writing: the first sentences state the conclusion or request. The **pyramid principle**, associated with Barbara Minto’s consulting writing, structures a document as a governing idea at the top supported by a small number of grouped arguments, each supported by evidence beneath it. Both are practitioner heuristics: widely used and logically defensible, not experimentally validated rules. Their rationale is that a reader who knows your conclusion can evaluate each piece of evidence against it instead of holding everything in mind until the end.

steps.label: Recommendation
steps.text: What you propose, in one or two sentences, with the decision you need and the deadline.

steps.label: Core reasons
steps.text: Two to four reasons, grouped so they do not overlap.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.text: For each reason, the strongest evidence and its quality.

steps.label: Risks and alternatives
steps.text: What would make you wrong, what you considered, why you rejected it.

steps.label: Next step
steps.text: Who does what by when if the decision is yes.

understand.title: Prerequisite: why order matters to a reader

blocks.text: Readers hold only a few ideas in mind at once while reading. If the purpose of a document is unknown, each paragraph must be stored until its relevance becomes clear. If the purpose is known, each paragraph can be checked against it and discarded or kept. That is the plain logic behind answer-first writing, and you can test it on yourself: notice how differently you read a report after someone tells you its conclusion.

understand.text: Audience analysis

Before choosing format or content, answer four questions about the audience: What decision can they make, and what is outside their authority? What do they already believe, and how strongly? What will they be held accountable for if this goes wrong? What vocabulary do they use? A chief financial officer, a head of clinical operations and a board each want a different first paragraph about the same proposal, not because the facts change but because their exposure does.

understand.caption: Audience analysis: their prior view versus their decision power
cells: Implementers who doubt the idea: listen first, show how their concerns shaped the plan, ask what would make it workable.
Decision-makers who doubt the idea: lead with the risk they fear most and how it is contained; offer a reversible first step.
Allies without authority: equip them with a short, accurate version they can repeat.
Sponsors: give them the decision, the trade-off and the language to defend it to others.

rows: Let a careful reader verify the reasoning and evidence, and find the weaknesses.
Narrative of how you did the work; findings that do not bear on the decision.
Let a decision-maker decide or ask the right question in five minutes.
Method detail, secondary reasons, most numbers except the decisive ones.

understand.text: Plain language helps every format: short sentences, concrete subjects and verbs, defined terms, numbers with units and comparisons, and hedges placed where the uncertainty actually is instead of scattered across every sentence. Precision and plainness are allies. “Expected to reduce soft-tissue injuries by roughly a quarter, with wide uncertainty because only two seasons of data exist” is both more honest and easier to act on than “may potentially contribute to improved outcomes.”

challenge.text: What “executive presence” research does and does not show

“Executive presence” is used in promotion discussions as if it were a measured trait: gravitas, confidence, composure, the ability to command a room. Most writing on it is practitioner work based on interviews and surveys of executives, and peer-reviewed research on presence as a distinct, validated construct is thin. You should treat specific prescriptions — how to stand, how fast to speak, what to wear — as practitioner advice of uncertain validity, and be alert to how “presence” can encode bias about accent, gender, age or cultural style.

Two well-supported lines of research help interpret what presence judgments are. The romance-of-leadership work shows that observers infer leadership from outcomes and salient impressions, especially under extreme results. The trust literature shows that people judge others on ability, benevolence and integrity. On that reading, “presence” is an observer’s inference that someone has sound judgment and can be trusted with consequences — an inference that clarity, composure under challenge and consistency can support, and that outcomes outside the person’s control can inflate or deflate.

Charisma — the nearest research construct to “presence” — sits inside the charismatic–transformational literature, which has large meta-analytic associations with follower outcomes. Van Knippenberg and Sitkin argue that these measures confound the construct with its effects, so ratings of a leader as inspiring may partly record that the team succeeded. The safest conclusion is that perceived charisma is associated with favorable outcomes, while whether a learnable “presence” causes those outcomes remains unsettled.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why presence is hard to study

blocks.text: To study presence causally you would need an agreed definition, a measure that observers apply consistently, and variation in presence that is not caused by the person’s status or success. Status itself changes how a speaker is perceived — the same sentence from a chief executive and an intern is heard differently — so correlations between presence ratings and seniority are hard to interpret. A study that shows senior leaders are rated higher on presence cannot tell whether presence led to seniority or seniority produced the ratings.
This is a recurring pattern in this course: a construct that feels obvious in daily life turns out to be hard to separate from the outcomes and status it supposedly explains.

challenge.text: Answer-first structure also has limits. With an audience that is strongly opposed, leading with the recommendation can trigger rejection before the reasoning is heard; some writers then open with the shared problem and the criteria for a good solution, and reach the recommendation quickly after. In some cultures and organizations, a direct opening reads as presumptuous. The principle survives — never make the audience hunt for your point — but the first sentence may need to establish common ground.

apply.text: A hypothetical state health agency must brief a legislative committee on why a vaccination outreach program missed its target. The analytical memo explains the data, the three counties driving the gap and the uncertainty in the estimates. The committee chair receives a one-page brief: the program missed by a stated margin, mostly in three counties because of clinic access, and the agency requests authority to move mobile clinics there by a date. The agency head’s 60-second answer to a hostile question opens with the request and one fact, then offers the brief.

In a hypothetical law firm, a partner advising a technology client’s general counsel on a contract dispute writes the recommendation in the first sentence — settle within a range — then the two reasons, then the litigation risk, and attaches the full analysis. The general counsel forwards only the first paragraph to her chief executive. The partner wrote that paragraph knowing it would travel alone.

In baseball operations, an analyst who recommends a change in how a club’s minor-league pitchers build workload faces several audiences at once: a director deciding on resources, coaches who will implement the plan and know the players, and a manager who cares about the major-league roster consequences. The memo lets a skeptical colleague check the model; the brief gives the director a decision and its main risk; the verbal version is what a coach repeats to a player. A recommendation that is right but legible only in the memo will not survive the trip from the meeting room to the bullpen.

apply.title: Executive twist: the unpopular recommendation with incomplete evidence

blocks.text: You must recommend to your superior that a respected program be paused, based on two seasons of data that suggest — but do not prove — it is not working. The program’s champion is in the meeting. Leading with “pause the program” is honest but may close the room; burying it is evasive. One defensible structure: state the recommendation and how confident you are in one sentence; name what the program’s champion has done well; give the single strongest piece of evidence and its weakness; propose a reversible step and the evidence that would change your mind. Clarity about uncertainty is not weakness; vagueness about the recommendation is.

retain.text: Executive communication puts the recommendation, its main reasons and the decision needed first, adapted to an audience’s decision rights and prior beliefs. BLUF and the pyramid are practitioner heuristics with a sound rationale. “Executive presence” is better treated as other people’s inference about judgment and trustworthiness than as a trait; the research that exists supports clarity and consistency, not posture.
