glossary.definition: The tendency of observers to explain organizational outcomes by pointing to leaders, strongest after extreme outcomes.
An observer’s inference that a person is or is not an effective leader, often drawn from outcomes and impressions rather than observed behavior.
A family of leader behaviors — articulating a vision, modeling values, stimulating and supporting followers — claimed to raise performance beyond expectations; its measurement is disputed.
A transactional leader behavior: agreeing on goals with people and recognizing or rewarding them when the goals are met.
The absence of leadership: avoiding decisions, being unavailable and not responding to problems; consistently associated with worse outcomes.
A perspective holding that leaders form relationships of different quality with different followers, and that relationship quality relates to outcomes.
A willingness to be vulnerable to another party based on the expectation that they will act in a way important to you, without your being able to monitor or control them.
The perceived characteristics that lead someone to trust another: ability, benevolence and integrity.
A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, such as admitting errors or raising concerns.
The theory that feedback works by directing attention, and that it helps less or harms when it draws attention from the task toward the self.
A practitioner technique of asking for suggestions about future behavior instead of evaluating past behavior; plausible but thinly researched.
The explicit degree of decision authority given to a person for a type of decision, from being told what to do to full ownership.
A practitioner writing convention, from U.S. military usage, that places the conclusion or request in the opening sentences.
A practitioner structure, associated with Barbara Minto’s consulting writing, that places a governing idea first, supported by grouped arguments and then evidence.
Working out an audience’s decision rights, prior beliefs, accountability and vocabulary before deciding what to say and in what order.
A popular term for the impression that a person has the judgment and composure of a senior leader; mostly described in practitioner writing rather than validated research.

exercise.title: Leadership Conversation Simulator

intro.text: You lead the analytics group of a regional health system (fictional). Marcus Ode, a senior data scientist, is your strongest technical contributor: his readmission-risk model is the reason the group has credibility with clinical leadership. He is also, by several accounts, dismissive of colleagues. Two analysts have asked to move off his projects. Nobody has filed a complaint. You have scheduled a one-to-one for Monday morning.

At each step, choose what you say or do. Four indicators move after each choice: **Trust** (Marcus’s confidence in your ability, benevolence and integrity), **Clarity** (whether the expectation is unmistakable), **Commitment** (whether he owns a specific change) and **Relationship risk** (the chance this ends in withdrawal, resentment or departure — lower is better). Feedback appears immediately. There is no single correct path; several endings are defensible, and each has a cost.
Notice where your choices put Marcus’s attention — on the task or on himself — and which part of trust each choice builds or spends.

text.text: Marcus sits down with his laptop open. “I only have twenty minutes — the validation run finishes at nine. What’s up?”

You have two concrete observations of your own: in last Tuesday’s code review he rejected three of a junior analyst’s suggestions with “that’s not how this works” and moved on; on Thursday he rewrote a colleague’s query without telling her. You also have second-hand reports.

choices.label: “I want to talk about how code reviews are going. Last Tuesday you rejected three of Ana’s suggestions without asking why she made them. I want to understand that, and I want it to change.”
choices.feedback: Direct and specific: the observation is yours and verifiable, so it keeps attention on behavior. The cost is a sharper start; he may hear it as an ambush, raising relationship risk.

choices.label: “Before anything else — how do you think the team is working together right now?”
choices.feedback: An open question signals that you want his view, which can build trust. It also delays the point; if he does not raise the issue, you will have to.

choices.label: “First, the readmission model is outstanding — clinical leadership loves it. There’s one small thing I want to mention about tone, and then more good news.”
choices.feedback: The praise sandwich buries the message between compliments. People quickly learn that praise announces criticism, which cheapens both, and “tone” is vague and self-focused rather than behavioral.

text.text: Marcus closes the laptop. “If her suggestions were correct I would have accepted them. Are you asking me to approve bad code to protect feelings?”

choices.label: “No. Your standards are the reason the model works. I’m separating the decision from the manner: reject what’s wrong, but ask one question first and give the reason. Right now people stop bringing you ideas.”
choices.feedback: You affirm what is legitimate (his standards — ability and integrity) while holding the behavioral expectation. Naming the cost to the work keeps the focus on the task, not on his character.

choices.label: “Several people have told me they find you dismissive. This isn’t just me.”
choices.feedback: Unnamed, aggregated complaints feel like a verdict he cannot answer. Attention moves to who said what — a self-focused, threat-heavy frame — and away from the specific behavior.

choices.label: “Fair point. Maybe I misread the review. Let’s just keep an eye on it.”
choices.feedback: Conceding the point you came to make removes the expectation entirely. It also costs integrity in his eyes: you raised something and abandoned it at the first resistance.

text.text: “Honestly? Slow. I’m carrying two projects and spending half my day fixing other people’s queries. Nobody else understands the validation framework.”

choices.label: “That’s useful, and I want to come back to the workload. I also saw something in Tuesday’s review that connects to it: you rejected three of Ana’s suggestions without asking why. That’s part of why people stop asking you for help early.”
choices.feedback: You acknowledge his concern and link it to the behavior with a specific observation. Connecting the behavior to a problem he cares about (being the bottleneck) gives him a task-focused reason to change.

choices.label: “Tell me more about the workload. What would help?”
choices.feedback: Listening may surface a real structural problem. If you never return to the behavior, though, the conversation becomes about his grievances alone.

text.text: Marcus looks puzzled. “Thanks. So what’s the actual issue? Did someone complain?”

choices.label: “Yes, there’s a real issue, and I should have led with it. In Tuesday’s review you rejected three of Ana’s suggestions without asking why. I want that to change.”
choices.feedback: Recovering from a soft opening is possible, and owning the miscue (“I should have led with it”) can earn credibility. The conversation now restarts on specific behavior.

choices.label: “No, nothing formal. Just be mindful of how you come across.”
choices.feedback: “How you come across” is about image, not behavior, and gives him nothing to do differently. Vague feedback is easy to agree with and easy to ignore.

text.text: A long pause. “So I’m the problem. I build the only thing in this department that works, and I’m the problem.”

choices.label: “You’re not the problem. Your work is the best on the team. One behavior is costing you influence and costing the team ideas. What would you need to make reviews work differently?”
choices.feedback: Separating identity from behavior lowers the threat to his self-image, and a question invites him to design the change — which tends to build commitment. Silence before answering would also have helped.

choices.label: “I’m not debating whether you’re valuable. This is a performance expectation. It will be part of your review this year.”
choices.feedback: Maximally clear and sometimes necessary. But moving to formal consequences while he is defensive makes the conversation about status and compliance; you may get changed behavior without changed attitude.

text.text: “Who? If people have a problem with me, they can say it to my face. Give me names.”

choices.label: “I won’t share names; I’d protect you the same way. Let me tell you what I saw myself, because that’s what I can stand behind.”
choices.feedback: Refusing names protects the people who spoke up — a signal to everyone that disclosure is safe — and shifting to your own observations makes the feedback verifiable.

choices.label: “It was mainly Ana and Jordan. I think you should talk to them.”
choices.feedback: Revealing who confided in you converts a feedback conversation into a confrontation and destroys the safety of the people who raised it.

text.text: Marcus nods, already glancing at his laptop. “Sure. I’ll be mindful. Anything else?”

choices.label: “Actually, yes. I wasn’t specific enough. In Tuesday’s review you rejected three suggestions without asking why. Next review, I want you to ask one question before rejecting anything.”
choices.feedback: Reopening a conversation you let slide is awkward but valuable. The request is now behavioral and checkable.

choices.label: “No, that’s it. Good luck with the validation run.”
choices.feedback: You leave with agreement to nothing in particular.

text.text: Marcus describes being pulled onto a second project by a vice president, without your knowledge, and being asked to “check everyone’s work” informally. It explains some of his irritation — and none of it was visible to you.

choices.label: “That’s on me to fix, and I will this week. Separately, the way reviews are going has to change, and the overload makes it more urgent: people stop asking you early, so you end up fixing more later. Can we agree on how reviews will work?”
choices.feedback: You take ownership of the structural problem — strong evidence of benevolence — and still hold the behavioral expectation, linking it to his own interest.

choices.label: “I had no idea. I’ll talk to the vice president today. Let’s not worry about the rest for now.”
choices.feedback: Fixing the workload builds trust, but dropping the behavior topic tells the two analysts who asked to move that nothing will change.

text.text: Marcus is calmer. “Fine. I can ask before I reject things. But if the code’s wrong, it’s wrong.”

choices.label: “Agreed. So: in reviews you’ll ask one question before rejecting, and give the reason in writing. I’ll fix the extra project by Friday. Let’s check how it’s going in two weeks.”
choices.feedback: A specific, two-sided agreement with a review date converts goodwill into accountability. Your half of the bargain matters as much as his.

choices.label: “Great. I trust you to handle it.”
choices.feedback: Warm, but nothing is specified and nothing is scheduled. Good intentions decay without a follow-up.

text.text: Marcus is correct and cold in the morning stand-up. A colleague mentions that he updated his professional networking profile last night.

choices.label: Ask for fifteen minutes: “Yesterday I went to consequences quickly. The expectation stands, but I want you to know why it matters to me and what I’ll do on my side.”
choices.feedback: Repair after a hard conversation is a sign of benevolence, not weakness, as long as the expectation itself does not move.

choices.label: Leave it. The expectation is clear, and he is an adult.
choices.feedback: Clarity without repair can produce compliance — and quiet exit planning by the person whose work you most depend on.

text.text: Ana tells you reviews are “much better — he actually asks why now.” Another analyst says Marcus has gone quiet in reviews and comments much less, even on real errors.

choices.label: Tell Marcus specifically what improved and its effect, then ask about the silence: “I don’t want you to stop catching errors — that’s the point of you.”
choices.feedback: Specific, task-focused recognition reinforces the new behavior, and naming the over-correction keeps his standards in play. Withdrawal is a common response to criticism; catching it early matters.

choices.label: Take the quiet as success and move on.
choices.feedback: Silence can be withdrawal rather than improvement. Losing his error-catching would cost the team the very thing that made him valuable.

end-growth.title: Outcome: a harder, better working relationship

text.text: Over the next quarter Marcus’s reviews become more useful to the team, and one of the analysts returns to his project. He still argues hard, and you still have friction. The change is not a personality transformation; it is a specific behavior, an agreement on both sides, and a follow-up that caught an over-correction.
Cost: time, two uncomfortable conversations, and a commitment from you on workload that you now have to defend to a vice president.

Marcus’s reviews are polite and minimal. Complaints stop. So does much of his error-catching, and six months later he accepts an offer elsewhere. The expectation was clear and was met in letter; the relationship that made his best work available to the team did not survive.
This is a defensible outcome in some organizations — the behavior that harmed colleagues stopped — but its cost is real and was partly avoidable.

Marcus leaves the meeting unsure what, if anything, was asked of him. Within a month a third analyst asks to move projects. The two who raised the issue conclude that speaking up achieved nothing, and the next problem reaches you later.
Avoiding the hard sentence protected the relationship with one person at the expense of the team’s trust in you.
Marcus confronts both analysts that afternoon. One files a formal complaint, now naming you as well. The original behavior is no longer the main problem; your disclosure is.
Recovery requires a direct apology to the analysts and a change in how concerns are handled — and the team will remember how this went for a long time.
The meeting ends warmly and for two weeks reviews improve. Under deadline pressure the old pattern returns, and because nothing was agreed or scheduled, raising it again feels like starting over.
The conversation was not wasted — trust rose — but accountability needs a specific behavior and a date.

debrief.text: Look back at your path. Where did your choices put Marcus’s attention: on specific, verifiable behavior and the work, or on his identity and standing? Which part of trust — ability, benevolence, integrity — did each move build or spend? Did you end with a specific, two-sided agreement and a date?

No path maximizes every indicator. Directness raises clarity and early risk; inquiry builds trust and can lose the point; formal consequences secure clarity at the cost of commitment. Skilled leaders choose which cost to accept, and then repair.

The simulator embodies two ideas from this week. Feedback intervention theory predicts that messages pulling attention to the self — vague comments about “tone”, unnamed complaints, threats to status — tend to weaken or reverse effects, while specific task-focused messages with a next step help. The trust model predicts that conceding the point costs integrity, owning a structural problem builds benevolence, and protecting confidences preserves the team’s willingness to speak up.

What the simulator does **not** show: real people are less predictable than any branching script; the indicator movements are ordinal teaching heuristics chosen by the author, not measured effects; and the “right” balance depends on organizational context — employment law, the person’s history, the stakes of the deliverable — that a short scenario cannot hold. Use it to rehearse structure and notice trade-offs, not to forecast a person.

assumptions: All people and the organization are fictional.
Indicator effects are ordinal teaching heuristics (−2 to +2 per choice) grounded in the cited research and the author’s judgment, displayed in words; they are not predictions of behavior.
Relationship risk is scored so that lower is better; the other three indicators are better when higher.
Each path has between three and five decisions; endings depend on the path, not on indicator totals.
The scenario assumes no prior formal complaint or legal issue; a real case with a formal complaint would involve human resources and different obligations.

case.title: The Brilliant Analyst
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. The Bayshore Herons are an invented club; numbers are synthetic.

body.text: Mireille Soto, the assistant general manager of the Bayshore Herons, had three emails flagged when she arrived on Monday. One was from Lena Okafor, the club’s pitching research analyst, asking for twenty minutes “to get the workload plan back on track.” One was from Ray Delgado, the minor-league pitching coordinator, asking for the same twenty minutes “to talk about how this is being handled.” The third was from the farm director, Tom Haskell, and was a single line: “We need to decide something before spring training or we’ll decide by default.”

Okafor had joined the Herons fourteen months earlier from a biostatistics group at a pharmaceutical company. She was twenty-nine, careful, and fast. Within four months she had assembled the organization’s minor-league pitching data — pitch counts, bullpen sessions, strength-program logs, training-room visits — into a single dataset for the first time. Within nine months she had built a model that estimated how the pace of a pitcher’s workload increase related to time lost to arm-related injury, and she had used it to propose a new build-up plan for the club’s starting pitchers: slower early-season increases, more frequent lighter bullpen sessions, and individual caps adjusted for each pitcher’s prior-year volume.

Soto had read the technical appendix twice. It was the most rigorous piece of work the department had produced. Okafor had backtested the model on four seasons of the club’s own data, reported uncertainty intervals rather than single numbers, and listed the model’s limitations in a section most analysts would have left out. Her headline estimate was that the new plan would reduce days lost to arm injuries among minor-league starters by roughly a fifth, with an interval wide enough to include almost no effect.

The trouble started at the November development meeting. Okafor presented to the coordinators, the affiliate pitching coaches who had flown in, Haskell and Soto. Her deck ran to thirty-eight slides. The recommendation appeared on slide twenty-nine. Several coaches later told Haskell that the first twenty minutes felt like a statistics lecture. When Delgado asked how the model handled a pitcher who “looks fine in the data but you can see is tired,” Okafor answered that observational fatigue assessments had not been recorded consistently and so could not be evaluated. That was accurate. Then she added that the current build-up plan was “not defensible on the evidence we have.”

Delgado had designed the current plan nine years earlier. He was respected across the organization, had coached several of the club’s current major-league pitchers in the minors, and was known for knowing more about each pitcher’s family, temperament and history than anyone else in the building. He said little for the rest of the meeting. Afterwards, three coaches told Haskell they felt they had been accused of hurting pitchers.

Haskell brokered a compromise: the new plan would be piloted at one affiliate in the spring while the others continued with the existing plan. The Double-A pitching coach, Dev Anand, volunteered; he was younger, had worked with analysts before, and liked Okafor. The other affiliates’ coaches were told the pilot was optional for them, which most understood as permission to ignore it.

By the end of the season the pilot had produced exactly the kind of evidence nobody could use. The Double-A starters lost fewer days to arm injuries than the organization’s average, but there were only six of them, two had been on unusually light workloads the previous year, and one of the pilot pitchers had a significant elbow injury in August. At the other affiliates, a highly regarded prospect on the existing plan had missed half the season with a shoulder problem. Each side cited the case that supported it. Okafor wrote a careful memo explaining that the pilot was too small to be informative in either direction. Few people read past the first page, which described the data cleaning.

Over the summer the working relationship deteriorated in small ways. Okafor began sending her weekly workload reports directly to Haskell and Soto, copying the coordinators, because she felt her recommendations disappeared when they went through Delgado. Delgado told Haskell that the reports arrived “like report cards” and that coaches had stopped reading them. Anand, caught between them, told Soto privately that Okafor was right about the data and wrong about people, and that Delgado was right about people and had not looked at the data. Two other affiliate coaches told Soto they would be willing to try the plan if Delgado endorsed it, and would not if he did not.

Okafor, for her part, felt that she was being asked to be less right in order to be liked. In her own one-to-one with Soto in September she said, “I’ve been told to build relationships. I’ve bought coffee. I’ve sat in bullpens. Nobody tells the coaches to learn what a confidence interval is.” She had received an informal approach from another club’s research department. She had not said whether she was considering it.

Haskell laid out the options in an email to Soto. The club could adopt the new plan organization-wide, with the coordinators responsible for implementation; it could extend the pilot to two affiliates for another year with a design that might actually produce usable evidence; or it could set the plan aside and fold some of its elements, such as individual volume caps, into the existing plan under Delgado’s direction. Each choice had a cost. Mandating the plan risked a coordinator and several coaches who would carry it out without conviction, and possibly a resignation. Another pilot risked losing Okafor and another season of the status quo. Folding elements into the existing plan risked a diluted version that would fail and discredit the analysis.

Soto also had to decide something less visible: what Okafor’s role should be. One option was to pair her with Delgado formally, making both co-owners of the pitching plan, with joint authority over changes. Another was to give her a translator — an experienced coach with analytical training who would carry her work into the field. A third was to leave the structure alone and coach her directly on how to present, which she suspected Okafor would hear as being told the problem was her personality.

The general manager had told Soto he would support whatever she recommended, provided she could explain it to the owner in a paragraph. Soto opened a blank document and wrote at the top: “What problem am I actually solving?” Then she sat looking at it for a long time.

Arm injuries have many causes; no plan can prevent them, and small samples cannot settle which plan is better in a single season.
Delgado has no formal veto, but affiliate coaches follow his lead in practice.
Okafor’s outside approach is real but unconfirmed; Soto does not know how seriously she is considering it.
The budget for a translator role exists only if another open position is left unfilled.
questions: What problem is Soto actually solving — a question about evidence, a question about authority, or a question about relationships? How does your answer change the recommendation?
Use the ability–benevolence–integrity model to diagnose what Delgado and the coaches doubt about Okafor, and what Okafor doubts about them.
If the new plan is probably better, what is the cost of adopting it in a way that leaves the coordinator and coaches without conviction? How would you estimate that cost?
Rewrite the first two sentences of Okafor’s November presentation for the coaches in the room.
Which of the three role options for Okafor would you choose, and what would you say to her about it?

perspectives.title: Mandate the plan, but share ownership
perspectives.text: The evidence favors the new plan, and a year of further delay has a real health cost to pitchers. Soto adopts it organization-wide, but makes Delgado and Okafor joint owners with authority to adjust individual caps based on coaches’ observations, which are recorded from now on. This uses Delgado’s ability and gives him a stake; it accepts friction and a risk that he declines. The weakness: a reluctant co-owner can slow-walk the implementation.

perspectives.title: Run a real test before mandating
perspectives.text: The pilot taught the organization that a small, non-random test persuades nobody. Soto extends the plan to two affiliates with pitchers assigned by a rule both sides agree on in advance, outcomes defined in advance and a review date. This treats the disagreement as an evidence problem and gives Delgado a fair hearing. The weakness: another year of delay, a possibly departing analyst, and a sample that may still be too small.

perspectives.title: Fix the relationship first; the plan will follow
perspectives.text: Adoption failed because of how the work was introduced, not its quality. Soto keeps the existing plan for one more season but folds in individual volume caps, gives Okafor a coach-translator partner, and coaches her directly on presenting to a skeptical audience — while telling the coordinators explicitly that dismissing analysis is not an option either. The weakness: Okafor may hear this as a demotion, and a diluted plan may fail and be blamed on the analysis.

case.application: The same dynamic appears wherever a technically superior proposal meets an established practice with respected owners. In a hospital, a clinical data scientist who shows that a sepsis protocol could be improved meets senior nurses and physicians who designed the existing protocol and know patients the data do not capture. In a technology company, an engineer who proves that a deployment process is unsafe meets the team that built it and has kept it running for years. In each case the technical question — is the new approach better? — is necessary but rarely sufficient. Adoption depends on who owns the change, whether the existing experts’ knowledge is used rather than overruled, how the recommendation is framed for each audience, and whether the evidence is strong enough to persuade people who did not produce it.

questions.prompt: A hedge fund’s chief investment officer is widely praised as a strategic visionary after a year of exceptional returns driven largely by a sector-wide rally. Which inference does the romance-of-leadership research most directly warn against?

options.text: That the rally affected many funds
That the praise is evidence of unusual leadership quality
That returns can be measured objectively
That the officer’s team may also deserve credit

questions.explanation: Meindl and colleagues found that observers over-attribute outcomes to leaders, especially after extreme results. Praise generated by an extreme year is therefore weak evidence of leadership quality; it may mostly record the outcome.

optionFeedback.a: This is a reasonable inference and part of the correction, not the error.
optionFeedback.c: Measurability is not the issue; attribution is.
optionFeedback.d: Spreading credit is consistent with, not contrary to, the research.

questions.prompt: Which is the most serious threat to the conclusion the authors draw?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. “We surveyed 400 employees in 60 retail stores at the end of a sales year. Employees rated their store manager on a 20-item inspirational leadership scale (sample item: ‘My manager makes me want to give extra effort’) and rated their own work engagement. Inspirational leadership correlated r = .52 with engagement. We conclude that training managers in inspirational leadership will raise engagement.”

options.text: The sample of 400 employees is too small for a correlation.
Leadership and engagement were rated by the same employees, some items describe outcomes, and ratings came after the year’s results were known.
Retail is not a knowledge-work setting.
A correlation of .52 is too large to be plausible.

questions.explanation: The design combines common-source ratings, items that partly measure the outcome (extra effort), and ratings collected after results were visible — the conditions under which romance-of-leadership attributions and construct confounding inflate correlations. None supports a causal claim about training.

optionFeedback.a: Four hundred is adequate to estimate a correlation; the problem is what the correlation means.
optionFeedback.c: Setting limits generalization but is not the main threat to the internal conclusion.
optionFeedback.d: Large correlations are expected when the same people rate overlapping constructs; that is the problem, not implausibility.

questions.prompt: A meta-analysis reports an overall correlation of .44 between transformational leadership and a set of outcome criteria. What percentage of the variance in the criteria is statistically associated with transformational leadership? Round to one decimal place.
questions.working: Square the correlation: 0.44 × 0.44 = 0.1936, which is about 19.4% of variance. The remaining roughly 80.6% is associated with other factors, and the figure says nothing about causal direction.
questions.explanation: Squaring a correlation gives the proportion of variance shared by the two measures. A correlation of .44 is large for social science but leaves most of the variance unexplained, and it is a correlation, not an effect of leadership.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in this argument?

stimulus.text: “After our new chief nursing officer arrived, patient-satisfaction scores rose 12 points and nurse ratings of her ‘inspiring vision’ were the highest in the system. Clearly her transformational style caused the improvement, so we should require all nursing directors to complete her leadership program.”

options.text: Patient satisfaction is not an important outcome.
It infers a causal effect of a style from a before–after change and ratings that may reflect the improvement itself.
Nursing is too different from other fields for leadership research to apply.
Leadership programs never work.

questions.explanation: A before–after change has many possible causes, and ratings of “inspiring vision” collected after improvement may partly record the improvement. The argument also assumes that a program reproduces her behavior. Each step needs evidence.

optionFeedback.a: The outcome may matter a great deal; the inference is the problem.
optionFeedback.c: Leadership findings can transfer; the flaw is causal reasoning.
optionFeedback.d: Overcorrection: some programs may help; the argument simply does not show it.

questions.prompt: Which response most directly addresses the trust deficit described?

stimulus.text: A new chief technology officer at a fintech firm is respected for her engineering ability and is seen as scrupulously fair. Engineers nonetheless do not tell her about schedule risks. In interviews they say: “She’ll protect the launch date, not us. When the last team flagged a delay, they got the blame.”

options.text: Publish her technical credentials and past project results.
Visibly absorb the cost of the next reported delay — defend the team to the business and adjust the date — and say why.
Introduce a stricter, rules-based reporting policy.
Hire a coach to improve her presentation skills.

questions.explanation: Ability and integrity are not in doubt; benevolence is — whether she will protect the engineers’ interests at some cost to herself. Only behavior that costs her something on their behalf addresses that perception.

optionFeedback.a: Addresses ability, which is not in doubt.
optionFeedback.c: Addresses consistency of rules (integrity), not care for their interests.
optionFeedback.d: Presentation is not the issue engineers describe.

questions.prompt: A chief medical officer wants to know whether a surgical department is psychologically safe. Which observations are informative? Select all that apply.

options.text: Junior staff raise concerns about procedures during briefings, including to senior surgeons.
The department’s average satisfaction score is high.
Near-miss reports are filed regularly and discussed without blame.
Meetings are pleasant and rarely include disagreement.
The spread of answers on a speaking-up survey is narrow, with no subgroup reporting fear.
Senior surgeons describe their own errors in review meetings.

questions.explanation: Psychological safety shows in behavior — speaking up across status lines, reporting near-misses, leaders disclosing their own errors — and in whether all members, not just the average, feel safe. Satisfaction and pleasant meetings can coexist with silence on the issues that matter.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: You manage a talented senior associate at a consulting firm whose client deliverables are excellent but routinely late, forcing teammates to work weekends. You raised it vaguely once (“watch the timelines”). Nothing changed. A major deliverable is due in three weeks, and you have one 30-minute meeting with her before then.

options.text: Tell her she has a reputation for being unreliable and that it is affecting her promotion case.
Describe the last two late deliverables and their effect on the team, ask what drove the delays, and agree on interim check-in dates for the upcoming deliverable.
Say nothing and quietly assign a teammate to shadow her work.
Praise her quality at length so she is receptive, then mention timelines briefly at the end.

questions.explanation: Specific observations and their impact keep attention on the task; inquiry surfaces causes you may not know; and an agreed set of check-ins converts the conversation into accountability before the next deadline.

optionFeedback.a: Reputation and promotion pull attention to self and status, which feedback intervention theory predicts will provoke defensiveness.
optionFeedback.c: Avoids the conversation and erodes trust if discovered; it also teaches the team that the problem is tolerated.
optionFeedback.d: Burying the message repeats the vague feedback that already failed.

questions.prompt: A new regional manager at a hospital network has strong analytical judgment but no track record with budget decisions, which are hard to reverse. Rank these delegation approaches for her first budget cycle, best first.

options.text: “Decide the budget; tell me what you did at quarter end.”
“Give me your recommended budget and your reasoning; we’ll decide together, and I’ll explain any change I make.”
“Use last year’s budget; I’ll handle changes.”
“Decide, but check with me before you submit.”

questions.explanation: With sound reasoning but no track record on hard-to-reverse decisions, consulting her and explaining changes builds judgment and trust with low risk. “Decide but check” is a reasonable next step once her reasoning is visible. Telling her to repeat last year wastes her judgment and teaches nothing. Full delegation with quarter-end reporting puts an irreversible decision in untested hands.

questions.prompt: Rank these opening sentences for a one-page brief to a city manager, best first.

options.text: “I recommend contracting two private crews to clear the pothole backlog by October, at a cost within the current maintenance reserve; I need your approval at Tuesday’s meeting.”
“The pothole backlog reached its highest level in a decade this spring.”
“This brief describes our analysis of road-maintenance data from 2019 to 2025.”
“Road maintenance is a complex issue involving many stakeholders and trade-offs.”

questions.explanation: The first states the recommendation, cost frame and decision needed. The second states the problem, a useful second sentence. The third describes process rather than the point. The fourth is empty context that could open any brief.

questions.prompt: How should you open the presentation?

stimulus.text: You will present a recommendation to replace a manual claims-review process at an insurer with a model-assisted one. The decision-maker, the head of claims, built the manual process and is skeptical. She has authority to approve or reject; her main concern, she has said, is wrongful denials that would create regulatory exposure.

options.text: Start with the model’s accuracy statistics and technical architecture.
Lead with how the proposal controls wrongful denials — human review of every model-flagged denial and a reversible three-month pilot — then the recommendation and its benefits.
Lead with the cost savings, since executives care about money.
Avoid stating a recommendation, and let her draw her own conclusion from the data.

questions.explanation: For a skeptical decision-maker with authority, the opening should address the risk she fears most and offer a reversible step, then state the recommendation quickly. Audience analysis — her decision power, prior view and accountability — drives the order.

optionFeedback.a: Technical detail answers a question she has not asked and delays her concern.
optionFeedback.c: Savings do not address regulatory exposure, her stated concern; leading with them may signal that you discount it.
optionFeedback.d: Withholding the recommendation forces her to do the synthesis and reads as evasive.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the following opening into an answer-first paragraph (60–100 words) for the chief executive of a regional hospital. Original: “Over the past two quarters, the quality team examined discharge data, interviewed staff on three units, and benchmarked against published readmission literature. A number of factors appear to be associated with readmissions, including medication reconciliation and follow-up scheduling. Several options could be considered going forward.” Assume the team recommends a pharmacist-led medication review at discharge on the two highest-readmission units, at modest cost, starting next quarter.
questions.modelAnswer: I recommend starting a pharmacist-led medication review at discharge on our two highest-readmission units next quarter, at modest cost within the existing pharmacy budget. Our two-quarter review found that medication-reconciliation errors were the most common factor we could act on quickly. The main risk is that pharmacist time is diverted from inpatient work; we would start on two units and review results after one quarter before expanding. I need your approval by the end of this month to schedule staff.

rubric.criterion: Recommendation and decision needed appear in the first sentence or two
levels: 1 — Recommendation and the decision requested are both in the opening

rubric.criterion: One clear reason and one risk, stated plainly
levels: 0 — No reason, or reasons and risks are vague
1 — A specific reason and a specific risk with its mitigation

rubric.criterion: Fits the audience and length; no invented facts
levels: 0 — Process narrative, jargon or invented figures
1 — 60–100 words, plain language, uses only the information given

reserve.prompt: In the Judge and Piccolo meta-analysis, what was notable about contingent reward, a transactional behavior?

options.text: It was unrelated to outcomes.
Its overall validity was close to that of transformational leadership and stronger for several criteria.
It was the strongest negative predictor.
It was not measured.

reserve.explanation: Contingent reward had an overall validity of .39, close to transformational leadership’s .44, and was the stronger predictor for several criteria — a reminder that clear expectations and follow-through matter as much as inspiration.

optionFeedback.a: It was substantially related to outcomes.
optionFeedback.c: Laissez-faire leadership was the negative predictor (−.37).
optionFeedback.d: It was one of the central dimensions analyzed.

reserve.prompt: What is the most reasonable interpretation?

stimulus.text: A software division’s climate survey shows high average psychological safety. In the same quarter, an outage post-mortem reveals that two engineers had noticed the faulty configuration a week earlier but did not raise it because the change belonged to the division’s most senior architect.

options.text: The survey proves the team is safe; the engineers were simply careless.
The average may mask low safety for junior members on issues involving high-status colleagues; the incident is more diagnostic than the average.
Psychological safety is irrelevant to outages.
The architect should be removed.

reserve.explanation: Team averages can hide subgroups who do not feel safe, especially when status differences are involved. A concrete failure to speak up is strong evidence about the climate for that kind of disclosure.

optionFeedback.a: Treats an average as proof and blames individuals for a predictable climate effect.
optionFeedback.c: Speaking up about risks is exactly what the construct concerns.
optionFeedback.d: Jumps to a personnel decision without understanding how disclosure was handled.

reserve.prompt: A coaching vendor cites a study in which coached managers rated their own leadership effectiveness much higher after six months. What is the most important limitation?

options.text: Six months is too long.
Self-reported outcomes from people selected for coaching, with no comparison group, cannot separate coaching effects from selection, attention and rating bias.
Managers cannot be coached.
Coaching meta-analyses show no average effect.

reserve.explanation: The design lacks a comparison group, relies on self-report and involves selected participants — the weaknesses that make coaching effects hard to estimate. Meta-analyses show positive average effects, but individual vendor studies like this one add little.

optionFeedback.a: Duration is not the main problem.
optionFeedback.c: Overstated; the evidence suggests positive average effects.
optionFeedback.d: Incorrect; meta-analysis reports positive average effects, from an imperfect literature.

reserve.prompt: You have 60 seconds in an elevator with a federal agency’s deputy director, who will decide next week whether to fund your data-sharing pilot. What should you say first?

options.text: A summary of the data architecture.
The request and its single most important benefit, then the one risk she is likely to worry about and how it is handled, then a request to send a one-page brief.
A history of how the project began.
Several statistics showing the scale of the problem.

reserve.explanation: A 60-second verbal version must leave the listener with the request, one reason and the next step. Detail belongs in the brief you offer to send.

optionFeedback.a: Technical detail cannot be absorbed by ear in 60 seconds and does not tell her what you want.
optionFeedback.c: History is the order of discovery, not decision.
optionFeedback.d: Several numbers by ear are hard to retain; one number at most, tied to the request.

assignment.title: One Recommendation, Three Ways

brief.text: Executives rarely fail to communicate because they lack information. They fail because the same recommendation must reach different people, with different time and attention, in different forms — and each form needs to do a different job without changing the substance. This assignment asks you to write one strategic recommendation three times.

Choose a recommendation you could plausibly make: from your own work (remove anything confidential, team-specific or identifying, and use synthetic numbers), or use the case for this week, The Brilliant Analyst, and write as Mireille Soto recommending a course of action to the general manager. Then produce three versions:

items: **A comprehensive analytical memo** (600–900 words, exhibits optional) that lets a careful, skeptical reader verify your reasoning and see its weaknesses.
**A one-page executive brief** (250–400 words) that lets a decision-maker decide, or ask the right question, in five minutes.
**A 60-second verbal explanation** (about 150 words; 130–165) written as a script you would actually say, then read it aloud and time it.

brief.text: Each version is graded on its own terms: a memo is not a long brief, and a verbal script is not a short memo. Finish with a short note explaining what you cut between versions and why. Draft in the Executive Communication Studio, which shows word counts, speaking time, sentence length and hedge words as you write. Those metrics are format checks only; they do not grade content.

assignment.deliverable: Three versions of one recommendation — a 600–900-word memo, a 250–400-word brief and a 130–165-word verbal script — plus a short note on what you cut and why.

template.heading: Analytical memo — Recommendation
template.guidance: The recommendation, the decision needed and the deadline in the first two sentences.

template.heading: Analytical memo — Context and analysis
template.guidance: The problem, two to four grouped reasons, and the strongest evidence for each with an honest note on its quality.

template.heading: Analytical memo — Risks, alternatives and decision needed
template.guidance: What would make you wrong, the alternatives you considered and why you rejected them, and the next step if approved.

template.heading: One-page executive brief
template.guidance: 250–400 words. Recommendation, the one or two decisive reasons, the main risk and its mitigation, the decision and deadline. No method detail.

template.heading: 60-second verbal script
template.guidance: 130–165 words. The request, one reason, one risk if needed, and the next step. Short sentences; at most one number. Read it aloud and record your time.

template.heading: What I cut and why
template.guidance: 80–150 words. Which material moved or disappeared between versions, and how each audience shaped those choices.

rubric.criterion: Analytical memo: rigor, structure and honesty about evidence

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Recommendation and decision needed open the memo; reasons are distinct and well grouped; evidence quality is stated honestly; risks, alternatives and what would change the recommendation are specific.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Answer-first with sound reasons and evidence; risks and alternatives present but somewhat general.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recommendation appears late or reasons overlap; evidence asserted without judging its strength; risks thin.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Follows the order of discovery; recommendation unclear; no risks or alternatives.

rubric.criterion: One-page brief: decision-ready in five minutes

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Within 250–400 words; a decision-maker could act or ask the right question from it alone; only the decisive reasons and numbers survive; decision and deadline explicit.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear and short; one or two items could be cut or the decision requested could be sharper.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Reads as a compressed memo; method detail or secondary reasons crowd the decision.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No clear recommendation or decision; exceeds a page or omits the main risk.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: 130–165 words and timed near 60 seconds; a listener would remember the request, one reason and the next step; sentences are short and speakable; at most one number.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Within range and clear; one sentence or figure is hard to absorb by ear.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Written prose rather than speech; several numbers or qualifications; the request is not memorable.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Outside the range or without a clear request.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Same recommendation and same claims in all three; shorter versions omit, never add or overstate; uncertainty is preserved proportionately.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Consistent recommendation; minor shifts in emphasis or confidence.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Shorter versions overstate certainty or introduce claims absent from the memo.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Versions recommend different things or contradict each other.

rubric.criterion: Audience fit and reflection on cuts

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Each version anticipates its audience’s decision rights and main concern; the note explains specific cuts with clear audience reasoning.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Audience considered in each version; note explains cuts in general terms.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Audience implicit; note lists cuts without reasons.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No evidence of audience analysis; note missing.

scenario.text: Write one recommendation in three formats. If you use this week’s case, you are Mireille Soto, assistant general manager of the fictional Bayshore Herons, recommending to the general manager what to do about the pitching workload plan and the analyst’s role. Otherwise, use a recommendation from your own work with all confidential or identifying details removed and synthetic numbers.
Write the memo first, then compress. The metrics below are format checks only; they do not judge content.

audience.cares: A clear recommendation he can defend to the owner in a paragraph; the main risk; what it costs.
Whether the decision protects players and the club’s investment, and whether the department is functioning.
Pitchers’ health, coaches’ standing, and whether his knowledge is used rather than overruled.
Whether the evidence is taken seriously and whether her role is a promotion, a demotion or a partnership.
What changes on the field, who decides individual cases, and whether they will be blamed for outcomes.

checklist: Recommendation and decision needed appear in the first two sentences of every version.
Each reason is distinct; none overlaps another.
Evidence quality is stated honestly, and uncertainty sits where it actually is.
The main risk and how it is contained are named.
Shorter versions omit material; they never add claims or increase certainty.
The verbal script contains at most one number and no sentence you would stumble over aloud.
Each version anticipates its audience’s decision rights and main concern.
No confidential, team-specific or identifying information; numbers are synthetic.

prompts: Think of a leader whose reputation you helped form. How much of your judgment rested on outcomes, and how much on behavior you directly observed?
What is the most important piece of bad news someone could be withholding from you right now? What have you done in the last month that raised or lowered the price of telling you?
In the simulator, which cost did you accept most readily — clarity, trust, commitment or relationship risk? Is that your pattern in real conversations?
Read the first paragraph of the last recommendation you sent. If the reader stopped there, would they know what you wanted?

review.front: What is the romance of leadership, and when is it strongest?
review.back: Observers’ tendency to explain outcomes by pointing to leaders; strongest after unusually good or bad outcomes.

review.front: Overall meta-analytic validities in Judge & Piccolo (2004) for transformational, contingent reward and laissez-faire leadership?
review.back: .44, .39 and −.37 — and contingent reward was stronger for several criteria.

review.front: Name the four problems van Knippenberg & Sitkin identified in charismatic–transformational research.
review.back: No clear definition; underspecified causal model; construct confounded with its effects; measures that do not reproduce the theorized structure.

review.front: What does squaring r = .44 tell you?
review.back: About 19% of variance is shared — large for social science, but most variance is elsewhere, and direction is unknown.

review.front: Three factors of trustworthiness in Mayer, Davis & Schoorman?
How is trust defined in the integrative model?
review.back: A willingness to be vulnerable to another party without being able to monitor or control them.
A shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — asking, admitting errors, raising concerns.

review.front: In Edmondson (1999), what mediated the link between psychological safety and team performance?
Why can a high average safety score mislead?
review.back: Averages hide subgroups — often lower-status members — who do not feel safe and may hold the key information.
Feedback helped on average, but a substantial share of feedback interventions reduced performance.

review.front: Why does feedback backfire, per feedback intervention theory?
review.back: It draws attention from the task to the self, so effort goes to protecting self-image.

review.front: Common root of “he went around me” / “she second-guessed me” disputes?
review.back: An unstated delegation level — no agreement on who decides and when to report.

review.front: Five steps of the difficult-conversation structure?
review.back: Purpose, observation, impact, inquiry, agreement (with a review date).
Recommendation and decision needed, core reasons, evidence, risks and alternatives, next step.

review.front: What does research support about executive presence?
review.back: Little as a validated construct; related work suggests it is an observer’s inference shaped by outcomes, status and judgments of trustworthiness.

preview.text: This week treated leadership as relationships: trust, candor, feedback and clear communication. Week 6 widens the lens to power — formal and informal authority, coalitions, and how to introduce change without destroying the relationships it depends on; the stakeholder thinking behind audience analysis becomes a full influence map. Week 7 returns to difficult conversations as negotiation. Week 8 turns delegation into organizational design, and the capstone in Week 14 asks for the memo and presentation formats you practiced here.
